interesting or the guy more enticing. Naturally,
wherever I went, there I was, with reality to face and
lessons to learn. When things did not turn out as I
expected (nearly always), I had to figure out how to
deal with the jolts and tremors.
In childhood, of course, the decision to move was
never mine. My father’s company would hand it down,
and off we would go again, to another branch in
another part of the country. Good-bye to friends and
houses, hello to new schools and kids and teachers,
hello to trembling knees and knots in my stomach until
I learned the way to my classrooms, until some of the
new kids became friends. Then, after a few years,
good-bye again.
The main purpose of the first paragraph of Passage A
(lines 1–6) is to:
A.
describe where the narrator and her family live.
B.
indicate the narrator’s frustration upon leaving
home.
C.
help establish the narrator’s identity as an
expatriate.
D.
provide specific information about the move the
narrator and her family made in 1992.
Which of the following statements most effectively
summarizes the main point of the fifth paragraph of
Passage A (lines 34–41)?
F.
The homesickness the narrator would feel upon
leaving California was difficult to endure.
G.
The narrator loved vacations when she was a
child, but eventually the excitement would wear
off.
H.
The narrator feels more at home on the coast than
she does in the desert.
J.
The familiarity of home is more desirable to the
narrator than the pleasures of vacation.
Which of the following quotations from Passage B most
effectively encapsulates a main theme of the passage?
A.
“We weathered five winters in northern
New England” (lines 57–58)
B.
“I have a feeling that this is not my last house”
(lines 64–65)
C.
“(And all the world’s a stage)” (line 68)
D.
“In childhood, of course, the decision to move was
never mine” (line 85–86)
In the context of Passage B, the fourth paragraph
(lines 73–84) mainly serves to:
F.
demonstrate that the narrator’s predilection for
moving began when she was in college and
continued as she tried to settle on a career.
G.
illuminate the narrator’s discussion of
peripeteia
and
anagnorisis
by providing details relating to
her own life.
H.
suggest that the narrator preferred living on her
own when she was in her twenties and thirties.
J.
explain why the narrator disagrees with the
perception that she is peripatetic.
The narrator of Passage B makes clear that the moves
she chose to make while she was in her twenties and
thirties often led to:
A.
unforeseen opportunity.
B.
extreme good fortune.
C.
unexpected challenges.
D.
needless caution.
Based on the last paragraph of Passage A (lines 42–48)
and the last paragraph of Passage B (lines 85–93),
which of the following statements best captures a
difference in the way the narrators describe the
prospect of moving away?
F.
The narrator of Passage A focuses more on the
effect that moving had on her siblings; the narrator
of Passage B focuses more on how moving
affected her.
G.
The narrator of Passage A focuses more on the
regret she felt upon leaving; the narrator of
Passage B focuses more on the apprehension she
felt upon going somewhere new.
H.
The narrator of Passage A focuses more on the
excitement of going to a new place; the narrator of
Passage B focuses more on the tedium of
constantly having to pack up and move.
J.
The narrator of Passage A focuses more on the
people she would miss after she left; the narrator
of Passage B focuses more on specific objects she
had to leave behind.
Based on the passages, both narrators attribute their
childhood moves to:
A.
changes related to their fathers’ work.
B.
their parents’ dissatisfaction with their children’s
schooling.
C.
pressure from their extended families.
D.
their parents’ desire for adventure.
